hints: Focus on the formula of the oxide each element forms in excess oxygen, as this controls the mole ratio.
Start with sodium: 0.100 mol Na makes 0.050 mol of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ with $M_r = 62.0$, giving 3.10 g.
Now apply the same moles to mass logic to MgO and to $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, remembering 4 P atoms are needed per mole of oxide.
walkthrough:
**Write the oxide formulas in excess oxygen**

Think about what each element makes when oxygen is plentiful. Sodium makes $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, magnesium makes $\text{MgO}$, and phosphorus makes $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ (often written as $\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$).

Balanced equations:
$$4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}$$
$$2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}$$
$$4\text{P} + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$$

**Check row 1, sodium**

From the equation, 4 mol Na gives 2 mol $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, so the ratio is 2:1. Start with 0.100 mol Na.

$$n(\text{Na}_2\text{O}) = 0.100 \times \frac{1}{2} = 0.0500 \text{ mol}$$
$$m = n \times M_r = 0.0500 \times (2 \times 23.0 + 16.0) = 0.0500 \times 62.0 = 3.10 \text{ g}$$
So row 1 is correct.

**Check row 2, magnesium**

Here the ratio is simple, 1 mol Mg gives 1 mol MgO. Start with 0.100 mol Mg.

$$n(\text{MgO}) = 0.100 \text{ mol}$$
$$m = 0.100 \times (24.3 + 16.0) = 0.100 \times 40.3 = 4.03 \text{ g}$$
So row 2 is correct.

**Check row 3, phosphorus**

This is the tricky one. 4 mol P atoms give only 1 mol $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$. Start with 0.100 mol P atoms.

$$n(\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}) = 0.100 \times \frac{1}{4} = 0.0250 \text{ mol}$$
$$m = 0.0250 \times (4 \times 31.0 + 10 \times 16.0) = 0.0250 \times 284.0 = 7.10 \text{ g}$$
So row 3 is also correct, and rows 1, 2 and 3 are all right.

options.A: All three masses match the calculation. Sodium gives 3.10 g of Na2O, magnesium gives 4.03 g of MgO, and phosphorus gives 7.10 g of P4O10. Well done for handling the different mole ratios carefully.
options.B: This misses out row 3. Many students doubt phosphorus because P4O10 looks complicated, or they wrongly use P2O5 with a 2:1 ratio but forget to halve the Mr as well. When done correctly with 4 P per P4O10, the mass is exactly 7.10 g.
options.C: This misses out row 2. Magnesium is actually the simplest case with a 1:1 ratio of Mg to MgO. Using Mr = 40.3 gives 0.100 x 40.3 = 4.03 g, so row 2 is correct.
options.D: This misses out row 1. Sodium forms Na2O, not NaO, so 0.100 mol Na gives only 0.050 mol of oxide. That gives 0.0500 x 62.0 = 3.10 g, so row 1 is correct.
